notes.definition: Diamond is a form of carbon with a giant covalent structure in which each carbon atom forms four strong covalent bonds with other carbon atoms. This makes diamond very hard, gives it a very high melting point, and means it does not conduct electricity.
explanation: Diamond is one of the forms of the element carbon. A carbon atom has four electrons in its outer shell. In diamond, each carbon atom uses all four of these outer electrons to form four covalent bonds, each with a different carbon atom. The four bonds point towards the corners of a tetrahedron, and every carbon atom is joined in the same way, building up a rigid three-dimensional network called a giant covalent structure. There are no separate molecules in diamond.

Diamond is very hard. To scratch, cut or break diamond, many strong covalent bonds must be broken, and each atom is held firmly in place in all three directions by its four bonds. There are no layers that can slide and no weak points in the structure. This is why diamond is the hardest natural substance and is used on the tips of drills and saws for cutting hard materials such as stone and glass.

Diamond has a very high melting point (above 3500 °C). Melting would require breaking a huge number of strong covalent bonds, which needs a very large amount of energy. There are no intermolecular forces in diamond, because there are no separate molecules; it is the covalent bonds themselves that must be overcome.

Diamond does not conduct electricity. To conduct, a substance needs charged particles that are free to move. All four outer electrons of every carbon atom are held in covalent bonds, so there are no delocalised electrons, and diamond contains no ions. This is an important contrast with graphite, the other giant covalent form of carbon, in which each carbon atom forms only three bonds and one electron per atom is delocalised.

When you explain a property of diamond in an exam, always link the property to the structure and bonding. Hardness and high melting point come from the many strong covalent bonds in the giant structure. Lack of conductivity comes from having no delocalised electrons (all four outer electrons are used in bonding) and no ions.
keyFacts: Diamond is a form of carbon with a giant covalent structure.
Each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds with four other carbon atoms.
The bonds are arranged tetrahedrally in a rigid three-dimensional network.
Diamond is very hard because many strong covalent bonds hold each atom in place.
Diamond has a very high melting point because many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it.
Diamond does not conduct electricity because it has no delocalised electrons or ions.
All four outer electrons of each carbon atom are used in bonding.
Diamond is used in cutting tools and drill tips because it is so hard.

keyTerms.definition: A form of carbon in which every carbon atom is covalently bonded to four other carbon atoms in a giant covalent structure.
A network of atoms all joined by strong covalent bonds, with no separate molecules.
A strong bond formed when two atoms share a pair of electrons.
The arrangement of four bonds around an atom pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron, as in diamond.
Electrons free to move through a structure. Diamond has none, so it does not conduct.

workedExamples.question: Explain why diamond does not conduct electricity.
steps: A carbon atom has 4 outer electrons.
In diamond each carbon atom forms 4 covalent bonds, so all 4 outer electrons are used in bonding.
This leaves no delocalised electrons, and there are no ions.
So there are no charged particles free to move and carry charge.
workedExamples.answer: Every outer electron is used in covalent bonding, so there are no delocalised electrons (or ions) to carry charge.

workedExamples.title: Counting bonds in diamond
workedExamples.question: In diamond each carbon atom forms 4 covalent bonds, and every bond is shared between 2 carbon atoms. How many covalent bonds are there in a sample containing 1000 carbon atoms (ignore atoms at the surface)?
steps: Count bond ends: 1000 atoms × 4 bonds each = 4000 bond ends.
Each bond has 2 ends (one at each of the 2 atoms it joins).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think diamond has strong intermolecular forces.
misconceptions.right: In fact diamond has no separate molecules, so it has no intermolecular forces. Its properties come from the strong covalent bonds throughout the giant structure.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think diamond conducts electricity because graphite does and both are carbon.
misconceptions.right: In fact in diamond each carbon atom forms four bonds, using all its outer electrons, so there are no delocalised electrons and diamond does not conduct.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often say diamond is hard because 'the bonds are hard to break' without saying what the bonds are.
misconceptions.right: In fact you must say that each carbon atom forms four strong covalent bonds in a giant covalent structure, so many bonds must be broken.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think diamond is made of large molecules of carbon.
misconceptions.right: In fact diamond is a giant covalent structure; a whole crystal is one continuous network, not a collection of molecules.

realWorld: Industrial diamonds are used on the edges of saws and the tips of drills to cut through rock, concrete and glass because diamond is so hard.
Diamond is used in jewellery because it is hard (so it does not scratch) and sparkles when cut.
Diamond-coated tools are used by dentists and surgeons for precise cutting.
examTips: Use the number: 'each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds'. Questions comparing diamond and graphite often hinge on four bonds versus three.
For hardness and melting point, say 'giant covalent structure', 'many strong covalent bonds' and 'a lot of energy needed to break them'.
For conductivity, say 'no delocalised electrons' (or 'all outer electrons are used in bonding'). Saying 'no free ions' alone is not enough.
Never mention intermolecular forces in an answer about diamond.
summary: Diamond is a giant covalent form of carbon.
Each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms.
Diamond is very hard: many strong covalent bonds hold the atoms rigidly.
Diamond has a very high melting point: many strong covalent bonds must be broken.
Diamond does not conduct: there are no delocalised electrons or ions.
Its hardness makes it useful for cutting tools.

questions.question: How many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form in diamond?
markScheme: 1 mark: 4
questions.explanation: Each carbon atom uses all four outer electrons to form four covalent bonds. Three bonds per atom is graphite.

questions.question: Which word best describes the structure of diamond?
markScheme: 1 mark: Giant covalent
questions.explanation: Diamond is a giant covalent structure: every carbon atom is joined to others by covalent bonds in a continuous network.

questions.question: Which property makes diamond useful for the tips of drills?
options: It has a low melting point
markScheme: 1 mark: It is very hard
questions.explanation: Diamond is the hardest natural substance, so it cuts through hard materials. It is not slippery (that is graphite) and does not conduct.

questions.question: Diamond is made of atoms of which element?
markScheme: 1 mark: Carbon
questions.explanation: Diamond, graphite, graphene and fullerenes are all forms of carbon.

questions.question: Why does diamond have a very high melting point?
options: It has strong intermolecular forces between its molecules
Many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it
It contains delocalised electrons that hold the atoms together
markScheme: 1 mark: Many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it
questions.explanation: Diamond has no separate molecules, so there are no intermolecular forces. Melting requires breaking many strong covalent bonds.

questions.question: Why does diamond not conduct electricity?
options: Its atoms are too close together
Its covalent bonds are too strong
It has no delocalised electrons or ions
It is a compound, not an element
markScheme: 1 mark: It has no delocalised electrons or ions
questions.explanation: Conduction needs mobile charged particles. In diamond, all outer electrons are used in bonding, so there are no delocalised electrons, and there are no ions.

questions.question: Which statement about diamond is correct?
options: Each carbon atom is bonded to three others in flat layers
Diamond consists of separate C₆₀ molecules
Diamond is soft because the layers slide
Each carbon atom is bonded to four others in a three-dimensional network
markScheme: 1 mark: Each carbon atom is bonded to four others in a three-dimensional network
questions.explanation: In diamond the bonds point tetrahedrally to form a 3D network. Layers of three-bonded atoms describe graphite, and C₆₀ is a fullerene.

questions.question: What is overcome when diamond is scratched or broken?
options: Strong covalent bonds between carbon atoms
markScheme: 1 mark: Strong covalent bonds between carbon atoms
questions.explanation: Diamond is held together only by covalent bonds, so breaking or scratching it means breaking covalent bonds, which is very difficult.

questions.question: Silicon is in the same group as carbon and also forms a giant covalent structure like diamond, with each atom bonded to four others. Which property would you predict for silicon?
options: It is a gas at room temperature
markScheme: 1 mark: A high melting point
questions.explanation: With each atom joined to four others by covalent bonds in a giant structure, many strong bonds would need to be broken, so silicon should have a high melting point (it melts at 1414 °C).

questions.question: Which explanation best accounts for diamond being harder than graphite?
options: Diamond's covalent bonds are ionic in character
In diamond every atom is bonded in three dimensions with no weak forces between layers, whereas graphite's layers can slide
Diamond molecules are larger than graphite molecules
markScheme: 1 mark: In diamond every atom is bonded in three dimensions with no weak forces between layers, whereas graphite's layers can slide
questions.explanation: Graphite's layers are held only by weak forces and slide, while diamond's atoms are locked in a rigid 3D network of covalent bonds. Neither is made of molecules.

questions.question: Which property does diamond have?
markScheme: 1 mark: Very high melting point
questions.explanation: Diamond has a very high melting point. It does not conduct, is very hard and is insoluble in water.

questions.question: How many electrons are in the outer shell of a carbon atom?
markScheme: 1 mark: 4
questions.explanation: Carbon has electronic structure 2,4, so it has 4 outer electrons, which it uses to form 4 covalent bonds in diamond.

questions.question: How many of the outer shell electrons of each carbon atom in diamond are NOT used in covalent bonding?
markScheme: 1 mark: 0
questions.explanation: All four outer electrons are used in the four covalent bonds, leaving none free. This is why diamond has no delocalised electrons.

questions.question:
In diamond each carbon atom forms 4 covalent bonds, and each bond joins 2 carbon atoms.
Calculate the number of covalent bonds in a diamond crystal containing 6000 carbon atoms (ignore atoms at the surface).
markScheme: 1 mark: 6000 × 4 = 24 000 (bond ends)
1 mark: ÷ 2 = 12 000 bonds
questions.explanation: Each bond is counted twice if you multiply atoms by 4 (once from each atom it joins), so divide by 2: 6000 × 4 ÷ 2 = 12 000.

questions.question: A diamond crystal contains 2.0 × 10²⁰ carbon atoms. Using the same reasoning as for diamond (4 bonds per atom, each bond shared by 2 atoms), calculate the number of covalent bonds in the crystal. Give your answer in standard form.
markScheme: 1 mark: = 4.0 × 10²⁰
questions.explanation: There are two bonds per carbon atom overall (4 ÷ 2), so the number of bonds is 2 × 2.0 × 10²⁰ = 4.0 × 10²⁰.

questions.question: Name the type of bond between carbon atoms in diamond.
markScheme: 1 mark: covalent
questions.explanation: Carbon atoms share pairs of electrons, forming covalent bonds.

questions.question: Give one use of diamond.
markScheme: 1 mark: cutting tools / drill tips / saw blades / jewellery
questions.explanation: Diamond's hardness makes it ideal for cutting tools; it is also used in jewellery.

questions.question: Explain why diamond is very hard.
acceptedAnswers: each carbon forms four covalent bonds
markScheme: 1 mark: each carbon atom forms four (strong) covalent bonds / giant covalent structure
1 mark: (rigid network so) many strong bonds must be broken to scratch or break it
questions.explanation: Hardness comes from the rigid network of strong covalent bonds, with no planes of weakness.

questions.question: Explain why diamond has a very high melting point.
markScheme: 1 mark: (giant covalent structure with) many strong covalent bonds
1 mark: which need a lot of energy to break
questions.explanation: Name the bonds and link them to the large amount of energy required.

questions.question: Explain why diamond does not conduct electricity.
acceptedAnswers: all outer electrons used in bonding
markScheme: 1 mark: each carbon atom forms four bonds / all outer electrons are used in bonding
1 mark: so there are no delocalised (free) electrons (or ions) to carry charge
questions.explanation: A complete answer explains why there are no delocalised electrons, not just that there are none.

questions.question: A student says: 'Diamond has a high melting point because it has strong intermolecular forces.' Explain why this is wrong.
markScheme: 1 mark: diamond has no separate molecules / is a giant covalent structure, so there are no intermolecular forces
1 mark: melting requires breaking strong covalent bonds
questions.explanation: Intermolecular forces only exist between separate molecules. Diamond is one continuous network.

questions.question: Compare the structure and bonding of diamond with that of silicon dioxide, and explain why both are very hard.
acceptedAnswers: each C bonded to four C
each Si bonded to four O
markScheme: 1 mark: both are giant covalent structures
1 mark: diamond contains only carbon atoms, each bonded to 4 C; silicon dioxide contains Si and O, each Si bonded to 4 O (each O to 2 Si)
1 mark: in both, every atom is held by strong covalent bonds, so many bonds must be broken to scratch them
questions.explanation: The structures are similar in type (giant covalent, four bonds per main atom) but differ in the elements present.

questions.question: State whether diamond is an element or a compound.
markScheme: 1 mark: element
questions.explanation: Diamond contains only carbon atoms, so it is an element (a form of carbon).

questions.question: Describe the structure and bonding in diamond and use it to explain why diamond is used in cutting tools.
markScheme: Indicative content: diamond is a form of carbon; giant covalent structure; each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds with four other carbon atoms; tetrahedral arrangement; rigid three-dimensional network; strong covalent bonds; to cut, scratch or break diamond many strong covalent bonds would need to be broken; so diamond is very hard; harder than the material being cut; high melting point means it does not melt from heat produced by friction during cutting.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear description of the structure (four bonds per carbon, giant covalent) linked to hardness and its use in cutting tools.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as 'diamond is hard' or 'strong bonds' with limited link to structure.
questions.explanation: Good answers include the specific number of bonds, the giant covalent structure, and link hardness to the need to break many strong bonds.

questions.question:
Diamond and graphite are both forms of carbon with giant covalent structures.
Explain the properties of diamond in terms of its structure and bonding, and explain why diamond does not conduct electricity whereas graphite does.
markScheme: Indicative content: diamond: each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds; with four other carbon atoms; giant covalent structure; rigid 3D tetrahedral network; very hard because many strong covalent bonds must be broken to scratch it; very high melting point because a lot of energy is needed to break many strong covalent bonds; insoluble; does not conduct electricity because all four outer electrons are used in bonding so there are no delocalised electrons and no ions. Graphite: each carbon atom forms only three covalent bonds; in layers of hexagonal rings; one outer electron per carbon atom is delocalised; delocalised electrons can move through the layers and carry charge; so graphite conducts.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed and coherent explanation of at least two properties of diamond, each linked to structure and bonding, with a clear comparison of the electrons in diamond and graphite explaining conductivity.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains some properties of diamond with reference to covalent bonds and gives a partial explanation of the difference in conductivity.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about properties or bonding, with little explanation.
questions.explanation: The decisive comparison is four bonds per carbon in diamond (no delocalised electrons) versus three in graphite (one delocalised electron per atom).

questions.question: Which statement about the solubility of diamond in water is correct, and why?
options: It dissolves, because carbon is a non-metal
It dissolves, because water breaks the covalent bonds
It does not dissolve, because water molecules cannot break the strong covalent bonds of the giant structure
It does not dissolve, because diamond contains ions
markScheme: 1 mark: It does not dissolve, because water molecules cannot break the strong covalent bonds of the giant structure
questions.explanation: Diamond is insoluble: the strong covalent bonds holding the network together are not broken by water. Diamond contains no ions.
